<strong>Que ce soit sur son groupe de so: Whether she is in her Facebook support group, at the Joujouthèque Saint-Michel, at the Table de concertation des organismes au service des personnes réfugiées et immigrantes or speaking at Halte-Femmes Montréal-Nord, Mariana Infante never loses her radiant smile. It is the smile of a woman who has lived through the worst: rape, psychological violence, physical violence, then forced exile… to survive. A profile.
Entourée de jouets destinés au prêt, Mar: Surrounded by toys meant for lending, Mariana Infante oversees the cleaning and checking carried out by several immigrant workers to restore these objects to their former glory. She welcomes me to a service point of the Joujouthèque Saint-Michel, a community organization dedicated to families, tucked above a Maxi grocery store. There, between a Barbie and a toy race-car track, she agrees to share her story with La Converse.
Arrivée du Mexique enceinte et avec un f: She arrived from Mexico pregnant, with a five-year-old son in her arms, having fled her husband's beatings to seek asylum in Quebec. Today, she is fighting to improve the support offered to immigrant women who are victims of domestic and sexual violence. These women, who face difficulties tied both to their immigration status and to their often very painful histories, are abandoned by Quebec society, made invisible.
C’est ce constat implacable, ce silence: It is this unflinching reality, this silence in which all these lives are walled in, that Mariana breaks every day, one swing of the pickaxe at a time. So that, unlike her, these women do not fall back into their abuser's trap.
Alors que les femmes immigrantes représe: Immigrant women make up 7% of Quebec's population, according to the Conseil du statut de la femme, and they are 13.6 times more likely to be victims of domestic violence, according to Statistics Canada; yet little progress has been seen in how they are supported. The community sector denounces this political paralysis, and tries to make up for it with very limited resources.
Dans les 46 centres d’hébergement membre: In the 46 shelters that belong to the Regroupement des maisons pour femmes victimes de violence conjugale, victims born outside Canada account for 69% of residents in the Montréal region. The figure is all the more alarming given that the interpreting service for victims of domestic violence could face a major disruption in June. The program was granted a reprieve from April to June 2024, but is still waiting to find out whether the Quebec government will renew its funding.
Comme l’écrit Virginie Cresci, journalis: As journalist and author Virginie Cresci writes in her essay Le prix des larmes : Le coût caché des violences sexuelles (to be published in Quebec in June, editor's note): “For some, committing oneself to the fight against violence, for justice, and against denial is the only way to face these traumas.” That is indeed the case for Mariana Infante. Convinced that she would not have fallen back into her ex-husband's hands had she received appropriate support, she works every day to help allophone immigrant women who are victims of domestic and sexual violence.
Mariana multiplie les actions. Elle a no: Mariana takes action on many fronts. Among other things, she created a support group on Facebook that connects victims with psychologists, lawyers and specialized organizations. Volunteers also help them move, for example.
« Ces femmes sont traumatisées et arrive: “These women are traumatized and arrive in a system they know absolutely nothing about, not to mention the language barrier, which can be enough on its own to keep them from breaking their silence. That's why it's important to help them by directing them to professionals who are used to these kinds of situations and know how to act, or simply to people who have a car and can help them carry their belongings,” she says.
La quarantenaire est également formatric: The woman in her forties is also a trainer for the Table de concertation des organismes au service des personnes réfugiées et immigrantes, in addition to working as a counsellor and facilitator at Halte-Femmes Montréal-Nord with women who have experienced violence.
« Il est de notre responsabilité de fair: “It's our responsibility to make an effort to help these women; we can't let them down. Even today, despite everything, I live with a knot of fear in my stomach. I've been here for six years, and my ex-husband keeps harassing me. He even wrote to my son telling him to rape my new partner's daughter!” Mariana says in alarm. The survivor is waging a deep-rooted fight, with a determination equal to the atrocities she survived. In front of her co-workers, Mariana tells her story without holding back.
Mariana Infante est née sous le soleil d: Mariana Infante was born under the Mexico City sun exactly 40 years ago. “My birth, in itself, was already complicated, because I was born of a rape. I had no idea, but my mother ended up telling me when I was 15, because I kept asking her questions. It was a real shock to find out, I had never imagined it, especially since I'm the oldest of four children and my mother never made any difference between us…” she recalls. It was a first trauma, followed by many others that would mark her life, and from which she would draw her strength.
Deux ans plus tard, Mariana rencontre ce: Two years later, Mariana met the man who would change her life forever. A brilliant, diligent student, the 17-year-old was studying computer programming. Despite the bullying she endured in this Mexican “patriarchal society,” which looks very unfavourably on children of single mothers like hers, she aspired to become a doctor.
« Je l’ai rencontré la première fois au: “I first met him at the youth centre. Then I ran into him again in a park where I was playing soccer with friends. When I wanted to go home, he followed me, him and one of his friends,” Mariana explains.
Quatre mois – c’est le temps qu’il aura: Four months: that is how long it took this predator, five years her senior, to get what he wanted: Mariana. “He started taking up all my time. I understood later that he had drawn up a real hunting plan. In four months, he turned my head around: he told me I was intelligent, that I deserved better… Like all narcissists, he presented himself as a perfect man, and then he started controlling me,” recalls the woman who would go on to have four children with him.
Mariana tentera bien de se sortir de son: Mariana did try to break free of his hold. But Daniel knew how to exploit the young woman's naturally compassionate nature. Now in a relationship with him, she barely glimpsed the other side of this man when she discovered she was pregnant. It had taken only one time… “I had never had sex. I'm very religious and, for me, marriage is very important. He pressured me so much that I gave in, and I got pregnant the very first time. I was in denial, unable to tell my mother. Meanwhile, he promised me we would get married and start a family,” she says.
C’est le début de la « descente aux enfe: It was the beginning of the “descent into hell.” When Mariana was seven months pregnant, Daniel and his father told the young woman that she would no longer be going back to her mother's and would now have to live with them. For her mother, whom she would not go to see because she was so ashamed of what was happening to her, her father-in-law made up a story that her daughter no longer wanted to see her.
« J’étais prise au piège. La violence ph: “I was trapped. Physical violence was added to the psychological violence from the very first days. After two weeks, I wanted to go home, and there was a barrage of blows, even though I was seven months pregnant. I was no longer allowed to attend my classes, and I couldn't leave the house except with him,” Mariana says in a hushed voice, her eyes misty. In the end, at 18, she gave birth alone in the hospital, where she suffered “obstetric violence.” One more ordeal.
Pendant les premières années de son fils: During the first years of her son Daniel, named after his father, Mariana experienced some respite. “We started a clothing business, at first at markets, then in two retail locations. I spent a lot of time at church, I was isolated, I had none of my friends from before him. Eventually, I got married, pushed by the church, and I got pregnant with my second child, when my first was five years old,” she says.
Mais un nouveau coup dur la frappe lorsq: But another blow struck when she discovered, on Valentine's Day, that her husband was having an affair with a customer. She found the strength to leave him. But when he learned that she had contacted his mistress, who then left him in turn because she thought he was separated, her husband took revenge on her. “He came to my place, pushed me to the ground and unleashed all his anger on me. I curled up in a fetal position and took the kicks, the punches… Until he ended up waking our son, who asked him why he was hitting his mommy. He stopped and left,” Mariana confides, tears still flowing.
Enceinte, elle passe plusieurs jours à l: Pregnant, she spent several days in the hospital. When she got out, she went to the police station, with the support of her family, with whom she had reconnected. Her complaint would vanish, like so many others in this Mexican society that protects abusers and holds that a woman should stay with her husband, whatever the cost. “I understood that the only solution was to leave the country,” she says with regret.
Commence alors une partie d’échecs pour: A chess match then begins, as she tries to leave with her husband's mandatory consent. Thanks to her mother and Daniel's father, he ended up agreeing to sign an authorization for her to leave the country. He thought she was going to spend some time at her mother's, who had settled in Canada.
Maria Infante est arrivée sur le sol qué: Maria Infante arrived on Quebec soil in the spring. “When I landed at the Montréal airport, the immigration officer saw my papers with the complaint, a letter from a psychologist… and he asked me questions. He's the one who explained that, given my situation, I could claim asylum and that the YMCA could help me. My mother-in-law was waiting for me at the exit. I told her I wasn't leaving with her,” she recalls.
Elle découvre alors un nouveau pays dont: She then discovered a new country whose language she did not speak and whose codes she did not master. Pregnant and accompanied by her five-year-old son, Mariana was taken in at the YMCA Residences for refugees and asylum seekers. “It was a shock. I was the only woman on the floor and, once, I found a man waiting for me in my room. Luckily, I was only there for 17 days, because I got help finding an apartment,” she remembers.

Livrée à elle-même, elle trouve un peu d: Left to fend for herself, she found some support from a neighbouring couple and gave birth to Victor. But her in-laws gave her no respite. Her sister-in-law moved in with her for several months. “They were harassing me, I was living on social assistance, because I wasn't entitled to daycare for my baby, so I couldn't work. I was scraping the bottom of the barrel at the end of every month, but despite everything, I made sure my children never went without,” Mariana says.
Après deux ans, elle parvient à convainc: After two years, she managed to convince the judge to approve her asylum claim: “It was one of the happiest days of my life! It's very hard to wait for a decision like that while learning the country's language, rebuilding your life, all while risking having to leave.”
Il s’agit d’une joie passagère, car quel: The joy was short-lived, because a few months later, the man who was still her husband showed up in Montréal. Stopped at the airport, he called Mariana and threatened to leave with the children. Cornered, she advised him to file an asylum claim of his own, so that he could enter the country. He then imposed himself in her home, where he lived for seven months before going back to Mexico, without having managed to convince her to follow him.
Ayant obtenu sa résidence permanente, el: Having obtained her permanent residence, she began working in hotels and took French-language integration courses. But her mother-in-law moved into the same building; Mariana found herself under constant pressure and surveillance. The vise tightened even more when the bishop of the parish she attended got in touch with the bishop of her husband's church and tried to convince her that he had changed and that family was more important than anything.
Accablée de toutes parts, Mariana doit e: Overwhelmed from all sides, Mariana also had to face the news of her mother's cancer; her mother was still living in Mexico. In 2013, she went back to the country and agreed to return to her husband, who was now attending church and paying for her mother's care. For Mariana, it was a choice made out of spite.
Elle tombe une nouvelle fois enceinte, d: She became pregnant once again and gave birth to a little boy, Angel, but the mirage of a normal family life vanished in an instant. “It was a nightmare! He took our passports, stopped going to church, stopped paying for my mother's care and kept me from being with her the day of her surgery. He also forced me to have sex, and that's how I got pregnant with my fourth child,” she says quietly.
Dépressive et se sentant coupable d’être: Depressed and feeling guilty for having gone back to Mexico, she bore the brunt of her husband's wrath. His violence was so extreme that it caused her to give birth prematurely at home. “My baby was born dead, strangled by the umbilical cord. Everyone told me it was over, but I made them leave and I did every rescue gesture I knew for long minutes, praying to heaven,” Mariana confides. Her determination saved her baby, little Elias, by “miracle.”
Sa famille l’aide alors à repartir, pour: Her family then helped her leave again, for good this time, by threatening to file a complaint for abduction and unlawful confinement. The only shadow over the picture was that she was forced to leave her youngest son behind, because his visa application had been refused.
Finalement, quelques mois plus tard, une: Finally, a few months later, one last ruse allowed her to pick up Elias at the Montréal airport while keeping her husband from crossing the border. “It was my second chance in Canada with my four children. From that moment on, I decided that nothing would stop me from dreaming anymore!” she says enthusiastically.
Après son retour en 2016, Mariana a pris: After her return in 2016, Mariana took her life into her own hands. She went back to school and earned a diploma in community development, while starting to work at the Joujouthèque Saint-Michel, where she still works. “This new start finally opened my eyes. I had to live through all of that to find the strength to live alone here. Today, I try to help others with my experience,” Mariana says. She has cut ties for good with her ex-husband and her in-laws.
Amoureuse, épanouie dans son travail, fi: In love, fulfilled in her work, proud to watch her four boys grow up, she is finally living the peaceful life she long dreamed of.
